claim: Forty-nine participants (25 female, Mage = 28.04 years, SDage = 7.04) were recruited and consented to participate in an fMRI study.
source: Forty-nine participants (25 female, Mage = 28.04 years, SDage = 7.04) were recruited and consented to participate in an fMRI study designed to measure 'how pain and emotions are processed in the human brain and influenced by psychological factors'.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study sample size and demographics from the Methods section.

claim: The protocol was approved by the NIH's Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board (Protocol 15-AT-0132, PI: Atlas).
source: Participants provided informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, and the protocol was approved by the NIH's Combined Neuroscience Institutional Review Board (Protocol 15-AT-0132, PI: Atlas).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval from the Methods section.

claim: Nine participants who provided consent did not complete the experiment due to ineligibility based on calibration (n=4), technical failures (n=1), compliance with procedures (n=2), or anatomical abnormalities identified in a clinical scan (n=2).
source: Nine participants who provided consent did not complete the experiment due to ineligibility based on calibration (n=4) technical failures (n=1), compliance with procedures (n=2), or anatomical abnormalities identified in a clinical scan (n=2) and were not included in the current analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusions from the Methods section.

claim: The final sample included 40 participants (22 female; Mage = 27.00 years, SDage = 6.21).
source: The final sample included 40 participants (22 female; Mage = 27.00 years, SDage = 6.21).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the final sample size and demographics from the Methods section.

claim: Sample size was based on power analyses from previous studies and on a behavioral pilot experiment conducted prior to the fMRI study.
source: As detailed in our clinical protocol (15-AT-0132; https://clinicaltrials.gov/ identifier NCT02446262), sample size was based on power analyses from our previous studies and on a behavioral pilot experiment conducted prior to the fMRI study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample size justification from the Methods section.

claim: A minimum of 5–9 participants per group was needed to achieve 80–95% power to detect cue-based differences in pain, including reversals.
source: We computed the effect size of cue-based differences in reported pain in a sample of 12 participants (6 per group) and determined that we need a minimum of 5–9 participants to achieve 80–95% power to detect cue-based differences in pain, including reversals (data available upon request).
evidence: This is a direct statement about power analysis results from the Methods section.

claim: Twenty participants per group were included in the fMRI experiment.
source: We therefore included 20 participants per group in the fMRI experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of participants per group from the Methods section.

claim: Four participants were excluded from fMRI analyses due to excessive head motion or technical issues during the scan, leaving a final sample of 36 participants for fMRI analyses (18 Uninstructed Group, 18 Instructed Group).
source: Two participants in the Uninstructed Group and two participants in the Instructed Group were excluded from fMRI analyses due to excessive head motion or technical issues during the scan (see Procedure), leaving a final sample of 36 participants for fMRI analyses (18 Uninstructed Group, 18 Instructed Group).
evidence: This is a direct statement about fMRI sample exclusions from the Methods section.

claim: All 40 participants were included in behavioral analyses.
source: All 40 participants were included in behavioral analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavioral analysis sample from the Methods section.

claim: Thermal stimulation was delivered to the left (non-dominant) volar forearm using a 16x16 ATS contact heat thermode controlled with a Pathway pain and sensory evaluation system (Medoc Ltd, Ramat Yisha, Israel).
source: We delivered thermal stimulation to the left (non-dominant) volar forearm using a 16x16 ATS contact heat thermode controlled with a Pathway pain and sensory evaluation system (Medoc Ltd, Ramat Yisha, Israel).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the thermal stimulation apparatus from the Methods section.

claim: Each heat stimulus lasted 8 s and consisted of a 1.5 s on-ramp phase, a 5 s plateau phase, and a 1.5 s off-ramp phase.
source: Each heat stimulus lasted 8 s and consisted of three phases: a 1.5 s on-ramp phase in which the temperature of the thermode rose from 32 °C to the target temperature level, a 5 s plateau phase in which target temperature was maintained, and a 1.5 s off-ramp phase in which the temperature returned to 32 °C.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the heat stimulus parameters from the Methods section.

claim: Thermode placement was adjusted between each block of trials (i.e. every 12 trials) to avoid sensitization, habituation, and skin damage.
source: Thermode placement was adjusted between each block of trials (i.e. every 12 trials) to avoid sensitization, habituation, and skin damage.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the thermode placement procedure from the Methods section.

claim: Temperatures ranged from 36°C to 50°C, in increments of 0.5 °C, and were selected based on a thermal pain calibration conducted immediately prior to the experiment.
source: Temperatures ranged from 36°C to 50°C, in increments of 0.5 °C, and were selected based on a thermal pain calibration conducted immediately prior to the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the temperature range and calibration from the Methods section.

claim: Thermode temperature was maintained at 32 °C between trials.
source: Thermode temperature was maintained at 32 °C between trials.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the baseline thermode temperature from the Methods section.

claim: Physiological data, including electrodermal activity (EDA), respiration, electrocardiography, and peripheral pulse, were recorded from the left hand using Biopac recording equipment at a sample rate of 500 Hz.
source: Physiological data, including electrodermal activity (EDA), respiration, electrocardiography, and peripheral pulse, were recorded from the left hand using Biopac recording equipment and accompanying AcqKnowledge software (Goleta, CA) at a sample rate of 500 Hz.
evidence: This is a direct statement about physiological data collection from the Methods section.

claim: Participants recorded pain ratings using a trackball with their right hand.
source: Participants recorded pain ratings using a trackball with their right hand while EDA was recorded from the left hand and heat was applied to the left arm.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pain rating method from the Methods section.

claim: Prior to the fMRI experiment, all participants underwent an adaptive pain calibration procedure to identify each participant's pain threshold, tolerance, and the reliability of the temperature-pain association.
source: Prior to the fMRI experiment, all participants underwent an adaptive pain calibration procedure (Atlas et al., 2010; Mischkowski et al., 2019; Dildine et al., 2020; Amir et al., 2021) to identify each participant's pain threshold, tolerance, and the reliability of the temperature-pain association (i.e. r2; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the pain calibration procedure from the Results section, with citations to prior work.

claim: Four participants were dismissed prior to the fMRI portion of the experiment due to low reliability (n=3) or pain tolerance above 50℃ (n=1).
source: Consistent with our IRB protocol, four participants were dismissed prior to the fMRI portion of the experiment due to low reliability (n=3) or pain tolerance above 50℃ (n=1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about participant exclusions from the Results section.

claim: For each participant who continued to the fMRI phase, temperatures associated with ratings of low pain (M=42.04 °C, SE = 0.43), medium pain (M=44.71 °C, SE = 0.37), and high pain (M=47.30 °C, SE = 0.30) were identified using linear regression.
source: For each participant who continued to the fMRI phase, we used linear regression to identify temperatures associated with ratings of low pain (M=42.04 °C, SE = 0.43), medium pain (M=44.71 °C, SE = 0.37), and high pain (M=47.30 °C, SE = 0.30).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the calibrated temperatures from the Results section.

claim: There were no differences between groups in the reliability of the association between temperature and pain, as measured by r2 (M=0.803, SE = 0.022; p>0.2).
source: There were no differences between groups in the reliability of the association between temperature and pain, as measured by r2 (M=0.803, SE = 0.022; p>0.2), or in temperatures applied during the task (all p's>0.1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about group comparisons from the Results section.

claim: There were no differences between groups in temperatures applied during the task (all p's>0.1).
source: There were no differences between groups in the reliability of the association between temperature and pain, as measured by r2 (M=0.803, SE = 0.022; p>0.2), or in temperatures applied during the task (all p's>0.1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about group comparisons from the Results section.

claim: Bayesian model comparison indicated that the best model for pain as a function of heat intensity included fixed effects of Heat Intensity, Cue, Phase, and Group and all possible interactions, along with random intercepts and slopes for all factors.
source: Bayesian model comparison indicated that the best model included fixed effects of Heat Intensity, Cue, Phase, and Group and all possible interactions, along with random intercepts and slopes for all factors.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical model from the Results section.

claim: All models revealed significant effects of Heat Intensity, Cue, Phase, Cue x Phase, and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions across participants.
source: All models revealed significant effects of Heat Intensity, Cue, Phase, Cue x Phase, and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions across participants (see Table 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, referencing Table 1.

claim: A significant Group x Cue x Phase interaction and a significant Group x Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interaction were observed, likely driven by the critical medium heat trials.
source: We also observed a significant Group x Cue x Phase interaction and a significant Group x Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interaction, which were likely to be driven by the critical medium heat trials, as reported below.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Bayesian posterior estimates indicated that the effects of Heat Intensity, Cue x Phase interactions, and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions were practically significant with enough evidence to reject the null (<1% in ROPE).
source: Bayesian posterior estimates indicated that the effects of Heat Intensity, Cue x Phase interactions, and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions were practically significant with enough evidence to reject the null (<1% in ROPE), while the main effect of Phase supported the null (i.e. no effect of Phase; 99.8% in ROPE), despite being statistically significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Bayesian statistical results from the Results section.

claim: The main effect of Phase supported the null (i.e. no effect of Phase; 99.8% in ROPE), despite being statistically significant.
source: Bayesian posterior estimates indicated that the effects of Heat Intensity, Cue x Phase interactions, and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions were practically significant with enough evidence to reject the null (<1% in ROPE), while the main effect of Phase supported the null (i.e. no effect of Phase; 99.8% in ROPE), despite being statistically significant.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Bayesian statistical results from the Results section.

claim: All other effects were of undecided significance (i.e. not enough evidence to accept or reject the null).
source: All other effects were of undecided significance (i.e. not enough evidence to accept or reject the null); complete results are reported in Table 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about Bayesian statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Similar results were observed when analyses were restricted to pain ratings from the 36 participants with useable fMRI data.
source: We observed similar results when we restricted analyses to pain ratings from the 36 participants with useable fMRI data; see Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This is a direct statement about robustness of results from the Results section.

claim: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pain.
source: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pain (A), skin conductance responses (SCR; B), or pattern expression in the neurologic pain signature (NPS; C) or stimulus-intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS; D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on skin conductance responses (SCR).
source: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pain (A), skin conductance responses (SCR; B), or pattern expression in the neurologic pain signature (NPS; C) or stimulus-intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS; D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pattern expression in the neurologic pain signature (NPS).
source: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pain (A), skin conductance responses (SCR; B), or pattern expression in the neurologic pain signature (NPS; C) or stimulus-intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS; D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pattern expression in the stimulus-intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS).
source: There were no differences between groups in the effect of heat intensity on pain (A), skin conductance responses (SCR; B), or pattern expression in the neurologic pain signature (NPS; C) or stimulus-intensity independent pain signature (SIIPS; D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All outcomes showed robust effects of heat intensity.
source: All outcomes showed robust effects of heat intensity (see Tables 1–2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results from the Figure 2 caption.

claim: Whole-brain voxel-wise analyses revealed robust effects of variations in stimulus intensity on heat-evoked activation within brain regions involved in pain, controlling for group.
source: Whole-brain voxel-wise analyses revealed robust effects of variations in stimulus intensity on heat-evoked activation within brain regions involved in pain, controlling for group (E), which were confirmed with separate analyses within the Instructed Group (F) and the Uninstructed Group (G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Only the left hippocampus and right S1 showed significant group differences at corrected levels.
source: Only the left hippocampus and right S1 showed significant group differences at corrected levels (H).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Group differences in the left hippocampus and right S1 were driven by temperature-induced deactivation in the Uninstructed Group.
source: Differences were driven by temperature-induced deactivation in the Uninstructed Group, as depicted in G.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Heat-evoked autonomic responses during the experiment were analyzed, with SCR and pupil dilation both significantly influenced by Heat Intensity and exhibiting Heat Intensity x Cue X Phase interactions.
source: Next, we analyzed heat-evoked autonomic responses during the experiment. SCR and pupil dilation were both significantly influenced by Heat Intensity and exhibited Heat Intensity x Cue X Phase interactions (see Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Both Heat Intensity and Heat Intensity x Cue x Phase interactions had practically significant effects on SCR (<1% in ROPE).
source: Both factors had practically significant effects on SCR (<1% in ROPE), whereas Bayesian analyses of pupillary outcomes indicated that evidence was not sufficient to reject the null hypothesis (100% in ROPE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Bayesian statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Bayesian analyses of pupillary outcomes indicated that evidence was not sufficient to reject the null hypothesis (100% in ROPE).
source: Both factors had practically significant effects on SCR (<1% in ROPE), whereas Bayesian analyses of pupillary outcomes indicated that evidence was not sufficient to reject the null hypothesis (100% in ROPE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about Bayesian statistical results from the Results section.

claim: There was no meaningful effect of temperature on pupil dilation.
source: Because there was no meaningful effect of temperature on pupil dilation and the number of subjects with useable pupil data was substantially less than those with useable skin conductance, we focused on SCR in subsequent analyses of cue effects on physiological arousal.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results from the Results section.

claim: There was no main effect of Group on pupil dilation or SCR, nor any interactions between Group and Heat Intensity for either outcome.
source: There was no main effect of Group on pupil dilation or SCR, nor any interactions between Group and Heat Intensity for either outcome, suggesting that temperature effects on physiological arousal were similar regardless of whether individuals were instructed about contingencies (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Temperature effects on physiological arousal were similar regardless of whether individuals were instructed about contingencies.
source: There was no main effect of Group on pupil dilation or SCR, nor any interactions between Group and Heat Intensity for either outcome, suggesting that temperature effects on physiological arousal were similar regardless of whether individuals were instructed about contingencies (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the interpretation of results from the Results section.

claim: Robust intensity-related changes were observed within pain modulatory regions, including bilateral insula, striatum, dorsal anterior cingulate, thalamus, and other regions that did not differ between groups.
source: We observed robust intensity-related changes within pain modulatory regions, including bilateral insula, striatum, dorsal anterior cingulate, thalamus, and other regions that did not differ between groups (see Figure 2E–G and Figure 2—source data 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about fMRI results from the Results section.

claim: Robust expression of both the Neurologic Signature Pattern (NPS) and Stimulus-Intensity Independent Pain Signature (SIIPS) was observed as a function of temperature-related changes in both groups (all p's<0.001).
source: Consistent with this, we observed robust expression of both the Neurologic Signature Pattern (NPS; Wager et al., 2013) and Stimulus-Intensity Independent Pain Signature (SIIPS; Woo et al., 2017) as a function of temperature-related changes in both groups (all p's<0.001, see Table 2) and signature pattern expression did not differ by group (all p's>0.2; see Figure 2C&D and Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about fMRI results from the Results section, with citations to prior work.

claim: Signature pattern expression did not differ by group (all p's>0.2).
source: Consistent with this, we observed robust expression of both the Neurologic Signature Pattern (NPS; Wager et al., 2013) and Stimulus-Intensity Independent Pain Signature (SIIPS; Woo et al., 2017) as a function of temperature-related changes in both groups (all p's<0.001, see Table 2) and signature pattern expression did not differ by group (all p's>0.2; see Figure 2C&D and Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about fMRI results from the Results section.

claim: Variations in heat intensity were positively associated with increases in pain-related activation in pain-related regions regardless of whether individuals were instructed about contingencies.
source: Thus variations in heat intensity were positively associated with increases in pain-related activation in pain-related regions regardless of whether individuals were instructed about contingencies.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing fMRI results from the Results section.

claim: Positive effects of heat intensity on the bilateral striatum were observed that did not differ by Group.
source: Within value-related ROIs, we observed positive effects of heat intensity on the bilateral striatum that did not differ by Group, whereas the VMPFC showed significant Group differences, driven by negative associations between temperature and VMPFC activation in the Uninstructed Group, but not the Instructed Group (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ROI results from the Results section.

claim: The VMPFC showed significant Group differences, driven by negative associations between temperature and VMPFC activation in the Uninstructed Group, but not the Instructed Group.
source: Within value-related ROIs, we observed positive effects of heat intensity on the bilateral striatum that did not differ by Group, whereas the VMPFC showed significant Group differences, driven by negative associations between temperature and VMPFC activation in the Uninstructed Group, but not the Instructed Group (see Table 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ROI results from the Results section.

claim: There were no associations between heat intensity and amygdala activation.
source: There were no associations between heat intensity and amygdala activation.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ROI results from the Results section.

claim: There was a significant Group x Cue interaction on expectancy at baseline (F(1,38) = 8.959, p=0.005), driven by significant differences in the Instructed Group (p=0.0027) but not the Uninstructed Group (p>0.3).
source: Consistent with our manipulation, there was a significant Group x Cue interaction on expectancy at baseline (F(1,38) = 8.959, p=0.005), driven by significant differences in the Instructed Group (p=0.0027) but not the Uninstructed Group (p>0.3), as shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: There were no main effects of Group or Cue on expectancy prior to conditioning (all p's>0.1).
source: There were no main effects of Group or Cue prior to conditioning (all p's>0.1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Following the first acquisition block, a significant Group x Cue interaction was observed on expectancy ratings (F(1,38) = 7.102, p=0.011) as well as a main effect of Cue (F(1,38) = 31.195, p<0.001).
source: Following the first acquisition block, we collected a second set of expectancy ratings. We again observed a significant Group x Cue interaction (F(1,38) = 7.102, p=0.011) as well as a main effect of Cue (F(1,38) = 31.195, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Both groups reported higher expectancy with the high pain cue following the first acquisition block, but differences were larger in the Instructed Group (p<0.001) relative to the Uninstructed Group (p=0.003).
source: Post-hoc comparisons indicated that both groups reported higher expectancy with the high pain cue (see Figure 3A), but that differences were larger in the Instructed Group (p<0.001), relative to the Uninstructed Group (p=0.003).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Instructions and learning both modulated cue-based expectations about pain.
source: Thus, instructions and learning both modulated cue-based expectations about pain.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing results from the Results section.

claim: Bayesian model comparison indicated that the best model for cue effects on pain during acquisition included fixed effects of Group, Cue, and Trial, with random intercepts and random slopes for Cue and Trial.
source: Bayesian model comparison indicated that the best model included fixed effects of Group, Cue, and Trial, with random intercepts and random slopes for Cue and Trial.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical modeling from the Results section.

claim: All models indicated that participants reported higher pain when medium heat was preceded by high pain cues than low pain cues (main effect of Cue), and this effect was practically significant based on Bayesian modeling (0% in ROPE).
source: Consistent with other studies of expectancy-based pain modulation (Atlas et al., 2010; Wiech et al., 2014; Reicherts et al., 2016; Fazeli and Büchel, 2018; Michalska et al., 2018; Abend et al., 2021), all models indicated that participants reported higher pain when medium heat was preceded by high pain cues than low pain cues (main effect of Cue: see Figure 3B and Table 3), and this effect was practically significant based on Bayesian modeling (0% in ROPE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, with citations to prior work, shown in Figure 3B and Table 3.

claim: There was a significant Group x Cue interaction on pain during acquisition which was of undecided significance (8% in ROPE).
source: There was a significant Group x Cue interaction (see Table 3) which was of undecided significance (8% in ROPE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Both groups reported practically significant effects of Cue on pain prior to the first reversal, although effects were larger in the Instructed Group.
source: Importantly, post-hoc analyses within groups indicated that both groups reported practically significant effects of Cue on pain prior to the first reversal (see Figure 3B and Table 3), although effects were larger in the Instructed Group.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 3B and Table 3.

claim: A statistically significant Group x Cue x Trial interaction was observed, although this was of undecided significance (35.45% in ROPE).
source: We also observed a statistically significant Group x Cue x Trial interaction, although this was of undecided significance (35.45% in ROPE; see Table 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Cue effects increased over time in the Instructed Group, as did pain reports overall.
source: Post-hoc analyses within groups indicated that Cue effects increased over time in the Instructed Group (see Figure 3C and Table 3), as did pain reports overall, whereas there were no interactions with time in Uninstructed Group participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 3C and Table 3.

claim: There were no interactions with time in Uninstructed Group participants.
source: Post-hoc analyses within groups indicated that Cue effects increased over time in the Instructed Group (see Figure 3C and Table 3), as did pain reports overall, whereas there were no interactions with time in Uninstructed Group participants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Instructions and learning both shape pain prior to reversal, effects are somewhat larger in Instructed Group participants, and the dynamics of expectancy effects on pain may differ as a function of whether individuals learn from experience or instruction.
source: Together, these results indicate that instructions and learning both shape pain prior to reversal, that effects are somewhat larger in Instructed Group participants, and that the dynamics of expectancy effects on pain may differ as a function of whether individuals learn from experience or instruction.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing results from the Results section.

claim: A main effect of Phase (B=–2.03, p<0.001) was observed on expectancy rating difference scores, indicating that differential expectations varied as contingencies reversed.
source: We observed a main effect of Phase (B=–2.03, p<0.001), indicating that differential expectations varied as contingencies reversed, and significant Group x Phase interaction (B=4.12, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: A significant Group x Phase interaction (B=4.12, p<0.001) was observed on expectancy rating difference scores.
source: We observed a main effect of Phase (B=–2.03, p<0.001), indicating that differential expectations varied as contingencies reversed, and significant Group x Phase interaction (B=4.12, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Only the Instructed Group reported differences in expectation that varied significantly as a function of Phase, whereas the Uninstructed Group showed weaker variations in expectations as contingencies reversed.
source: Post-hoc analyses indicated that only the Instructed Group reported differences in expectation that varied significantly as a function of Phase, whereas the Uninstructed Group showed weaker variations in expectations as contingencies reversed (see Figure 4A and B).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: All models revealed significant Cue x Phase interactions on pain, indicating that cue effects on pain varied as contingencies reversed, and this effect was sufficient to reject the null hypothesis of no interaction (<1% in ROPE).
source: All models revealed significant Cue x Phase interactions on pain, indicating that cue effects on pain varied as contingencies reversed (see Figure 4C and D and Table 4), and this effect was sufficient to reject the null hypothesis of no interaction (<1% in ROPE).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 4C and D and Table 4.

claim: All models revealed main effects of Cue, such that individuals reported higher pain in response to the original high pain cue than the original low pain cue, and main effects of Phase, such that pain was higher on original contingencies relative to reversals, and these effects were significant in frequentist analyses but were of undecided significance based on Bayesian estimates.
source: All models also revealed main effects of Cue, such that individuals reported higher pain in response to the original high pain cue than the original low pain cue, and main effects of Phase, such that pain was higher on original contingencies relative to reversals, and these effects were significant in frequentist analyses but were of undecided significance based on Bayesian estimates (see Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Frequentist analysis approaches revealed significant Group x Cue x Phase interactions, driven by stronger reversals of Cue effects in the Instructed Group.
source: Finally, frequentist analysis approaches revealed significant Group x Cue x Phase interactions, driven by stronger reversals of Cue effects in the Instructed Group (see Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Post hoc analyses conducted separately by Group indicated nearly 100% probability of positive Cue x Phase interactions in each group, although evidence was only sufficient to reject the null hypothesis in the Instructed Group.
source: Post hoc analyses conducted separately by Group indicated nearly 100% probability of positive Cue x Phase interactions in each group, although evidence was only sufficient to reject the null hypothesis in the Instructed Group (see Table 4).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Similar results were observed when analyses were restricted to pain ratings from the 36 participants with useable fMRI data, although the Group x Cue x Phase interaction was marginally significant in frequentist approaches.
source: We observed similar results when we restricted analyses to pain ratings from the 36 participants with useable fMRI data, although the Group x Cue x Phase interaction was marginally significant in frequentist approaches; see Supplementary file 1 for complete details.
evidence: This is a direct statement about robustness of results from the Results section.

claim: Consistent findings were observed when the model was tested with a beta distribution, which was found to provide better fits based on posterior prediction.
source: We also observed consistent findings when we tested the model with a beta distribution, which was found to provide better fits based on posterior prediction (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about robustness of results from the Results section.

claim: Predictive cues shape pain perception even as contingencies change, whether or not participants are instructed about contingencies.
source: Thus predictive cues shape pain perception even as contingencies change, whether or not participants are instructed about contingencies.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing results from the Results section.

claim: Reversals may be slightly larger in participants who are explicitly instructed about contingencies, however group differences were not practically meaningful based on Bayesian statistics.
source: In addition, reversals may be slightly larger in participants who are explicitly instructed about contingencies and reversals, however group differences were not practically meaningful based on Bayesian statistics.
evidence: This is a direct statement summarizing results from the Results section.

claim: Heat-evoked SCRs were influenced by predictive cues on medium trials and reversed as contingencies changed, but the magnitude of these differences did not differ by Group.
source: Heat-evoked SCRs were influenced by predictive cues on medium trials and reversed as contingencies changed, but the magnitude of these differences did not differ by Group (see Figure 4D and Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about results from the Results section, shown in Figure 4D.

claim: While effects on heat-evoked SCR were statistically significant based on frequentist models, they were not sufficient to reject the null hypothesis of no difference based on Bayesian models.
source: While effects were statistically significant based on frequentist models, they were not sufficient to reject the null hypothesis of no difference based on Bayesian models (see Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement about statistical results from the Results section.

claim: Only 13 Instructed Group participants had variations in heat-evoked SCR on medium heat trials and were included in analyses.
source: Importantly, only 13 Instructed Group participants had variations in heat-evoked SCR on medium heat trials and were included in analyses; we therefore take these results with caution and did not analyze associations between trial-by-trial SCR and brain responses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about sample size limitations from the Results section.

claim: Anticipatory arousal was associated with a main effect of Cue and a significant Group x Phase interaction, but no interactions between Cue and Phase were observed, suggesting that anticipatory responses did not vary as contingencies change.
